<!-- Scope of the call-site dispatch change, measured 2026-09-23 by a delegated worker on main 20a884410, JDK 25, compiler path. Every run had a private -Dfortress.caches outside the repository; no tracked source was modified. The shadow is scope/scope-shadow.patch, applied after the dispatch probe's shadow/shadow.patch (rung P's -Dprobe.rungP switch): OverloadSet.java (-Dprobe.scope=off|callsite|skip) and OverloadingChecker.scala (-Dprobe.spSentence=off|own|lifted). Commands: scope/scope-run.sh. Captures under scope/: *.compiled.txt, dispatch-probes.compiled.txt, javap-template.txt, prelude-compare.txt, compiler-tests.txt, sentence-library.txt, sentence-corpora.txt, walk.txt. The zero probe's library stack is rebuilt on the current tree: its two memo hunks are dropped (the tree has its own since d28cf74d0), its five api edits give way to the tree's repair (a7ced6764), and QQ's comprises is written as that stack had it (§5). -->

# The dispatcher taking the call site's static arguments: sized in a shadow

**The answer.** The generic dispatcher is already loaded under the call site's static arguments; only its arms ignore them. Making each generic arm use the dispatcher's own static parameters is one file, one edited function and three new helpers: 43 code lines in `OverloadSet.java`, plus 1 for the switch and 3 for the variant that leaves generic arms out of a dispatcher that has no static parameters. `MieDispatchSub` then prints `Marker[Blue]`. The compiler prelude is byte-identical. The 43 compiler tests that declare generic overloads all print the same. Of the 34 that link, 31 have byte-identical classes and 3 differ only inside a generic dispatcher. Top-level functions only: generic dotted methods fail the same way and are not covered (`ScopeMethod`). Enforced, the specification's overload sentence refuses 179 declaration pairs in the library's apis under the narrower reading, 11 of them already errors today, and 6 gated compiler tests; a text scan finds 6 gated interpreter tests (§5).

## 1. How the compiled path handles generics today

- A **static argument** is the type that fills a generic's static parameter at one use. In `grab[\Blue\](b)` it is `Blue`. Usually nobody writes it: the checker infers it from the declared types at the call, so `b: Tag[\Blue\]` gives `X = Blue` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:912-930`).
- An **instantiation** is the generic with its static parameters replaced by static arguments: `grab[\Blue\]` is an instantiation of `grab[\X\]`.
- The compiler writes one *template* class per generic function, with `X` left in the names of the types it mentions (`Marker⟦X⟧`). The class loader stamps an instantiation from it when a class named with real arguments is first needed. For `grab⟦Blue⟧` it copies the template and rewrites every `X` in it to `Blue` (`runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java`, `MethodInstantiater.java`). The part of the name after `✚`, the template's arrow type, is never rewritten (`InstantiationMap.java:354`).
- A call that needs no choice at run time is compiled as a call to that named class. The checker's static arguments go straight into the name (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3670-3735`), so `grab(z)` with `z: Tag[\ZZ32\]` calls `grab⟦ZZ32⟧`.
- **Dispatch** is choosing at run time which declaration of an overloaded name runs, by the argument's actual type. A **dispatcher** is the method the compiler generates for that. It tests the argument against each declaration, most specific first, and calls the first that applies (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1303-1760`). One is generated for a declaration when some more specific declaration of the same name may apply at run time. If the least specific declaration is generic, the dispatcher is itself a template, named and loaded like any generic function: `grab⟦Blue⟧` at the call site (`OverloadSet.java:2005-2062`).
- **RTTI** (run-time type information) is the object every compiled value carries that describes its type. That includes the argument of each generic supertype, one per generic name: `Mixed`'s RTTI says `Sub` of `Red` and `Tag` of `Blue`.
- How a generic arm finds its static arguments today: it asks the value for its RTTI (`getRTTI`), asks that for the argument at the arm's generic (`Sub__1()`, giving `Red`), and passes the answer to `RTHelpers.loadClosureClass`. That call spells the instance's name from the RTTI's own Java class (`runtimeSystem/RTHelpers.java:160-178`, `runtimeValues/RTTI.java:53-58`), and the loader stamps it (`OverloadSet.java:1410-1728`). Inside a dispatcher template the arms do this too: they ignore the template's `X`, which the loader has already set to the call site's argument (`javap-excerpts.txt:60-80`).
- The authors weighed the question in a comment: "Some overloads have static args, but even if they are supplied, runtime inference is still necessary (so I think) -- drc 2010-02-24 / Not quite so -- if each static parameter is mentioned in any invariant occurrence, then the supplied type is exact" (`OverloadSet.java:1981-1990`).

## 2. The design

**What the specification says.** Declarations of one name share their static parameters (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-105`), so "static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable" (`:106-107`). The chapter assumes "that all static variables in functional calls have been instantiated or inferred" (`:136-138`), and they are "statically inferred from the context of the function call" (`expressions/var-ref.tex:37-40`). One set of static arguments, fixed at the call, therefore applies to every declaration. A declaration applies at run time if the value's type is a subtype of its parameter type at those arguments. For `MieDispatchSub`, `grab(b)` with `b: Tag[\Blue\]` fixes `X = Blue`. `Mixed` is not a `Sub[\Blue\]`, so the `Tag` declaration runs and the answer is `Marker[Blue]`.

**`MieDispatchAny`'s `grab(a)`, `a: Any`.** The specification refuses the program: `grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])` beside `grab(a: Any)` is an error "for one declaration to have static parameters and another to not have them" (`overloading.tex:103-105`). The question of which declaration runs therefore does not arise. If the sentence is not enforced, both readings give the same answer. The call was resolved to `grab(Any)`, which has no static parameters, so the call site supplies none. With no arguments to instantiate it, the generic declaration is not applicable. The code should refuse the pair at compile time (§5). Failing that, it should leave the generic arm out of such a dispatcher, which is the `skip` variant below. Either way `grab(a)` returns the `Any` declaration's `Red`.

**The three candidates.**
- **(a) The dispatcher gains the static arguments as parameters**, and every call site the checker resolved with static arguments pushes their RTTIs. This changes the signature of every dispatcher whose least specific declaration is generic, and the descriptor at every call site that reaches one. The template would then carry `X` twice, in its name and in its parameters. The arms would still be stamped through `loadClosureClass` from RTTI names, which keeps the `ZZ32` naming defect (§4). For `grab(Any)` it passes nothing, because that call site has nothing to pass. Not built.
- **(b) The call site loads an instantiated dispatcher named with the static arguments.** It already does, for every dispatcher that is a template (§1). The change is inside the template: each generic arm whose static parameters match the dispatcher's, up to renaming, is renamed into the dispatcher's parameters. It is then tested with a plain `instanceof Sub⟦X⟧` and called as `grab⟦X⟧` by name, and the loader turns both into `Blue`. Nothing is read from the value, and no signature, call site or template kind changes. This is the specification's model, one instantiation of the name fixed at the call, and it is the smallest of the three. Built.
- **(c) The arms keep reading from the value and skip on mismatch.** The template would need `X`'s RTTI in its body. A generic object's RTTI class reads its parameters' RTTIs from fields (`CodeGen.java:5686-5690`), but a function template has no such field, so this needs a new way to name it. Each arm would then compare the RTTI read from the value with it. Equality is wrong where `X` occurs only covariantly, because the value's argument can be a subtype of the call site's. The correct test is "read ⊑ call site" followed by instantiating at the call site's argument, and that is (b) with the reading left in. It changes every generic arm of every template dispatcher, keeps `loadClosureClass`, and keeps both defects of §4. Not built.

## 3. The size, measured

**The shadow** (`scope/scope-shadow.patch`, first file): `OverloadSet.java` only. In `generateCall` (`:1303`), a generic arm of a template dispatcher gets a `StaticTypeReplacer` from its static parameters to the dispatcher's (`atTemplateParams`). Its parameter and return types are built at those parameters, so they contain no variable of the arm's and take the existing no-inference path. The call goes to the arm's instance named with the dispatcher's parameters (`invokeArmAtTemplateParams`: the same stem the value-reading path passes to `loadClosureClass`, with the arm's name moved away from the dispatcher's as that path does, `:1650-1654`). Code lines: 2 imports, `templateStaticParams` 3, `atTemplateParams` 13, `invokeArmAtTemplateParams` 15, five edited lines in the type-structure loop, and 5 replacing 2 at the call: 43. ## 4. The two side defects

**A generic reached through a less specific declaration throws when its return type mentions the parameter.** The value-reading arm ends with a cast to the arm's declared return type, spelled with the arm's own parameter names (`OverloadSet.java:1720-1727`). In a dispatcher that is not a template, nothing rewrites `X`, so the cast is to the template class `Marker⟦X⟧` itself. `MieDispatchAny`'s `grab(a1)` throws this way under stock and `callsite` alike (`dispatch-probes.compiled.txt:31-32`, `:75-76`). The same cast also goes wrong inside a template whenever the arm names its parameters differently from the dispatcher: the loader rewrites only the dispatcher's names. Stock `ScopeArms` casts to an unrewritten `Marker⟦Y⟧` (`ScopeArms.compiled.txt:5-6`). Stock `ScopeAlpha2` gets its `Marker⟦B,A⟧` rewritten with the dispatcher's map to `Marker⟦Blue,Red⟧` (`ScopeAlpha2.compiled.txt:5`). No multiple instantiation is involved in either. **The change fixes it inside templates**: a renamed arm takes the no-inference path, whose call returns the right type without that cast, and both probes pass. It leaves the defect in non-template dispatchers (`MieDispatchAny` under `callsite`) and in dotted methods. `skip` removes that path, and the sentence makes it unreachable for top-level functions, because a set that mixes generic and non-generic declarations is refused.

**A `ZZ32` instantiation made at run time is spelled differently from the static one.** `loadClosureClass` spells each argument with `RTTI.className()`, the RTTI's own Java class: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$ZZ32` becomes `fortress|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32` (`RTHelpers.java:174-175`, `RTTI.java:53-58`). Static code spells `ZZ32` as `com|sun|fortress|compiler|runtimeValues|FZZ32` (`javap-excerpts.txt:6`). The dispatcher's value path is its only caller (`OverloadSet.java:1696`). `ScopeZZ32Sub` reaches it through a template with no multiple instantiation. Stock throws: `IntSub` is not a `Sub⟦fortress|CompilerBuiltin%ZZ32⟧` (`ScopeZZ32Sub.compiled.txt:5`). Under `callsite` the arm is named `grab⟦X⟧` inside the template, the loader writes the call site's own spelling, and it prints `SubM[ZZ32]` (`:10`). **The change avoids the defect on the template path and does not remove it.** `MieDispatchZZ32` and `MieDispatch`'s `grab(a)` still throw under `callsite` (`dispatch-probes.compiled.txt:81-82`, `:58-59`), and `skip` removes that path. The two spellings remain: the generated RTTI factories also build class names from `RTTI.className()` (`RTHelpers.getRTTIclass`, `:18-54`, called from `InstantiatingClassloader.java:2810`), untouched and unmeasured here.

## 5. What the specification's overload sentence refuses, measured

**The check.** It is in `checkOverloading`'s pair loop (`OverloadingChecker.scala:383`, before the existing rules; `scope-shadow.patch`, second file, 19 code lines). Two declarations of one name are refused when their static parameters differ in number, in kind, or in bounds after positional renaming. "Static parameters" has two readings for a functional method. Under `own` it is only the method's own list. Under `lifted` the trait's parameters come first, which is how the checker already builds its arrows for a top-level set (`STypesUtil.scala:123-127`). Like every rule of this checker, the check never sees a symbolic operator (`OverloadingChecker.scala:546-550`), and in a component it sees only declarations with a body (`:117-121`). The text scan `sentence-scan.py` counts both apart. On the two library apis it agrees with the checker exactly under `own` (179 of 179, none extra) and finds 326 of 335 under `lifted`.

**The interpreter's library.** `FortressLibrary.fsi` and `RangeInternals.fsi` were checked through the zero probe's stack (`scope/sentence-library.txt`). The stack needed three adjustments for the current tree. Its memo hunks are dropped, since the tree has had its own memo since `d28cf74d0`. Its five api edits give way to the tree's own repair of the same defects (`a7ced6764`). `QQ`'s `comprises { AnyIntegral, ... }` is written as the zero stack had it, because the tree's form stops the api's check with an earlier error. The stock run gives 203 errors, the triage's figure (`sentence-library.txt:4`).

| reading | pairs refused | of them the stock rules already refuse | whole-unit errors |
|---|---|---|---|
| `own` | 179 | 11 | 382 |
| `lifted` | 335 | 43 | 538 |

- The 43 are the triage's 35 plus the 8 it said the sentence also reaches (`perf-probes/nat/triage.md:52-59`). The other pairs are ones the stock rules accept.
- The 156 pairs found only under `lifted` are all a functional method of a generic trait beside one of the same name in another trait or object, most often its own implementation. Examples are `Integral[\I\]`'s twelve operators (`GCD`, `LCM`, `REM`, `MOD`, `DIV`, `CHOOSE`, four bit and two shift operators; 36 pairs) beside `ZZ32`'s, `ZZ64`'s and `NN64`'s. The `lifted` reading therefore refuses implementing a generic trait's functional method in a non-generic subtype, which the tower cannot survive. The triage families `CAP` (20), `seq` (6) and `MINMAX` (5) appear only under this reading.
- Symbolic operators add 329 pairs under `own` by the text scan (`sentence-corpora.txt`): `-` 116, `+` 53, `=` 47, `<` 25, `:` 25, `#` 25, `>=` 13, `>` 9, `<=` 9, `::` 6, and one `BIG //`. They are the same shapes.

The families under `own`, each with the rewrite that satisfies the sentence and what the interpreter does with it:
- **juxtaposition 80, DOT 48**: the tower's functional methods, which have no static parameters (`.fsi:271-520`, `:2360-2362`), beside the vector and matrix products. The api already pads every product to one list, `[\T extends Number, nat n, nat m, nat p\]` (`.fsi:1512-1647`); the component declares one to three (`.fss:2265-2642`). The only rewrites are padding the scalar side to the same four parameters or using another operator for one side. The interpreter loads the padded api today.
- **CMP 25**: comparison and tower methods (none) beside the tuple orders `CMP[\A,B\]` and `CMP[\A,B,C\]` (`.fsi:2495`, `:2501`). Rename the tuple orders, which the interpreter accepts.
- **MIN 8, MAX 8**: `StandardMin`/`Max`/`MinMax`, `Number` and `QQ` (none) beside the array-scalar block `[\T extends Number, I\]` (`.fsi:2556-2559`). Rename the array forms, which the interpreter accepts.
- **openRangeHelper 3, SCMP 3, PCMP 3**: one, two and three parameters for one to three dimensions (`RangeInternals.fsi:612-616`, `:30-40`). Pad each to three parameters, or rename by arity. The interpreter accepts padding (`ScopePad`, `walk.txt`).
- **__cond 1**: `[\E,R\]` and `[\E\]` (`.fsi:755-756`), the generator `if` with and without `else`, a name the desugarer emits (`WellKnownNames.java:65`). Pad the second with `R`; the interpreter accepts padding.

`ScopePad` is the padding repair in small: `pad[\A,B\](x: Box[\A\])` beside `pad[\A,B\](x: Box[\A\], y: Box[\B\])`. It passes the check and prints `one`/`two` compiled (`ScopePad.compiled.txt`) and under `walk`.

**The rest of the library and the builtins.** The compiler prelude compiled with the check on is refused nothing under either reading: `AnyType`, `CompilerBuiltin` and the three `Compiler*` libraries (`sentence-corpora.txt`). In the zero stack the apis `FortressBuiltin`, `AnyType`, `NatReflect`, `List` and `String` reach the check and are refused nothing (`sentence-library.txt:5-7`). `NativeArray`'s 44 earlier errors stop it before the check; the text scan finds nothing there. The other library files, by the text scan:
- `Generator2.fss:52-57`: `takeleft`, `takeright`;
- `Tuple.fsi:17-24`: `first`, `second`, `third`, one per arity;
- `QuickSort.fsi:16-20`;
- `QuickCheck.fss:728-734`: `__genMatchElse`;
- `Set.fss:76-79`;
- `CovariantCollection.fsi:14-16`: `APPCOV`;
- `Containment` under `lifted` only.

**compiler_tests/** (`sentence-corpora.txt`). The checker was run on 48 candidates: the 43 of §3, the text scan's hits under either reading, and every program declaring a name the prelude declares. It refuses 6 programs, the same 6 under both readings, and all are gated:
- `Compiled12.invariantInference` (14 pairs) and `invariantInference2` (8), both through `Compiled12.invariantInference.test`;
- `Compiled14`: `f[\T\]()` beside `f[\T extends ZZ32\](x: T)`, through `Compiled14.test`;
- `Compiled16f`: `g(x: String)` beside the functional method `g[\S extends ZZ32, U\](self)`, through `Compiled16.test`;
- `Compiled10.Comprehensions3`: two `__generate`, through `AfterTypeChecking.test`'s `typecheck`;
- `Compiled6.ak`: `XXX6ak.test` expects exactly two errors, and the check adds a third.

The judge named two of the six. `Comprehensions4` and `Compiled18` have earlier errors and never reach the check. A full sweep, stopped for time after the first 95 programs in name order, refused only `Comprehensions3` among them.

**tests/ and library_tests/**, by the text scan only. The checker cannot take them one at a time: the zero stack re-checks the whole library first, three minutes a run. Under `own`, 9 programs in `tests/` are hit:
- 6 are gated: `overloadTest8.fss:33-37`, `doubledOverloading.fss:36-41`, `GeneratorNullPointer.fss:18-20`, `ArrayListQuick.fss:36-55`, `PureListQuick.fss:36-55`, and `genericMethod4.fss:21-22`, whose dotted `g[\T\](t:T)` sits beside `g[\T, V\](t1:T, t2:T)` and which a column-0 grep cannot see;
- 3 are expected failures: `XXXgenericMethod1` to `3`.

`lifted` adds `fmTest3`. `library_tests/` has none.

## 6. Not settled

- **The specification is not uniform on when static arguments are fixed.** `overloading.tex:136-138` fixes them before applicability. `:173-175`, read alone, says of any "call f(C)", dynamic calls included (`:135-136`): "If the parameter type P includes static parameters, they are inferred as described in \chapref{type-inference} before checking the applicability of the declaration to the call". That is the interpreter's model. The chapter it cites is empty: "This chapter will include the Fortress static type inference mechanism." (`inference.tex:15`).
- **Which static parameters a functional method has.** The specification does not say. `lifted` refuses implementations of a generic trait's functional methods, and `own` does not; this note recommends neither.

(* Two static parameters, named in the opposite order by the more specific generic:
   pair[\B,A\](t: SubTwo[\B,A\]) is pair[\A,B\](t: SubTwo[\A,B\]) up to renaming.
   Through t: Two[\Red,Blue\] the call is checked as the Two generic at A = Red, B = Blue. *)
trait Two[\A,B\] end
trait SubTwo[\A,B\] extends Two[\A,B\] end
object Red end
object Blue end
object RedAndBlue extends SubTwo[\Red,Blue\] end
object PlainPair extends Two[\Red,Blue\] end
trait Marker[\A,B\] end
object TwoM[\A,B\] extends Marker[\A,B\] end
object SubM[\A,B\] extends Marker[\A,B\] end

pair[\A,B\](t: Two[\A,B\]): Marker[\A,B\] = TwoM[\A,B\]
pair[\B,A\](t: SubTwo[\B,A\]): Marker[\B,A\] = SubM[\B,A\]

name(m: Any): String = typecase m of
    TwoM[\Red,Blue\] => "TwoM[Red,Blue]"
    SubM[\Red,Blue\] => "SubM[Red,Blue]"
    else => "other"
  end

run(): () = do
  t1: Two[\Red,Blue\] = RedAndBlue
  println("pair(t1), t1: Two[Red,Blue] = RedAndBlue      -> " name(pair(t1)))
  t2: Two[\Red,Blue\] = PlainPair
  println("pair(t2), t2: Two[Red,Blue] = PlainPair -> " name(pair(t2)))
end
end
component ScopeArms
export Executable

(* MieDispatchSub with arms that can be told apart: the Tag generic returns a TagM, the
   Sub generic a SubM, both Markers.  The Sub generic names its parameter Y, so the
   dispatcher must rename it to the Tag generic's X.  Through b: Tag[Blue] the call is
   checked as the Tag generic at X = Blue and dispatched; the specification's answer is
   TagM[Blue] for Mixed (Sub[Blue] does not apply), SubM[Blue] for SubBlue, TagM[Blue] for
   TagBlue.  Mixed needs the relaxed checkP to link. *)
trait Tag[\X\] end
trait Sub[\X\] extends Tag[\X\] end
object Red end
object Blue end
object Mixed extends { Sub[\Red\], Tag[\Blue\] } end
object SubBlue extends Sub[\Blue\] end
object TagBlue extends Tag[\Blue\] end
trait Marker[\X\] end
object TagM[\X\] extends Marker[\X\] end
object SubM[\X\] extends Marker[\X\] end

grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\]): Marker[\X\] = TagM[\X\]
grab[\Y\](t: Sub[\Y\]): Marker[\Y\] = SubM[\Y\]

name(m: Any): String = typecase m of
    TagM[\Red\] => "TagM[Red]"
    TagM[\Blue\] => "TagM[Blue]"
    SubM[\Red\] => "SubM[Red]"
    SubM[\Blue\] => "SubM[Blue]"
    else => "other"
  end

run(): () = do
  r: Sub[\Red\] = Mixed
  println("grab(r), r: Sub[Red] = Mixed    -> " name(grab(r)))
  b1: Tag[\Blue\] = Mixed
  println("grab(b1), b1: Tag[Blue] = Mixed   -> " name(grab(b1)))
  b2: Tag[\Blue\] = SubBlue
  println("grab(b2), b2: Tag[Blue] = SubBlue -> " name(grab(b2)))
  b3: Tag[\Blue\] = TagBlue
  println("grab(b3), b3: Tag[Blue] = TagBlue -> " name(grab(b3)))
end
end
component ScopeZZ32Sub
export Executable

(* The ZZ32 naming defect reached through a generic dispatcher, with no multiple
   instantiation: IntSub is a Sub[ZZ32] only.  Through t: Tag[ZZ32] the call is checked as
   the Tag generic at X = ZZ32 and dispatched, and the Sub arm applies. *)
trait Tag[\X\] end
trait Sub[\X\] extends Tag[\X\] end
object IntSub extends Sub[\ZZ32\] end
trait Marker[\X\] end
object TagM[\X\] extends Marker[\X\] end
object SubM[\X\] extends Marker[\X\] end

grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\]): Marker[\X\] = TagM[\X\]
grab[\X\](t: Sub[\X\]): Marker[\X\] = SubM[\X\]

run(): () = do
  t: Tag[\ZZ32\] = IntSub
  println("grab(t), t: Tag[ZZ32] = IntSub -> " (typecase grab(t) of
      SubM[\ZZ32\] => "SubM[ZZ32]"; TagM[\ZZ32\] => "TagM[ZZ32]"; else => "other" end))
end
end

subtype relation instead of the substitutable relation.  This reflects
the restriction that receivers of dotted methods cannot be
coerced.  However, \KWD{self} parameters of functional methods can be
coerced.  This distinction is consistent with the intuition that
functional methods are rewritten into top-level functions.

Note that the only difference between applicability and applicability
with coercion is that substitutability is used instead of subtyping
to compare the parameter types of the declarations.

Also note that the definition of applicability with coercion does not
take keyword parameters or varargs parameters into account.  Such
declarations are conceptually rewritten into numerous declarations
which cannot be called with elided arguments nor with variable number of
arguments (as described in \secref{applicability-with-special-params}).  If
one of the expanded declarations is applicable with coercion to a call,
then the original declaration (with keyword or varargs parameters) is
applicable with coercion to the call.



\section{Coercion Resolution}
\seclabel{resolving-coercion}
For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a
declaration that is applicable without coercion.  If so, the most
specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are
explicitly added to the functional call.  If more than one coercion is
possible then the coercion that yields the most specific type is
chosen.  \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
\chapref{overloaded-declarations} describe overloading rules for the
declarations of coercions and overloaded functionals that guarantee
there exists always a most specific coercion when two or more are possible.

We first define a notion of more specific types in the presence of coercion.
Recall from \secref{type-relations} that Fortress defines an
\emph{exclusion} relation between types which is denoted by $\excludes$.

For types $T$ and $U$, we say that $T$ \emph{rejects} $U$,
and write $T \rejects U$, if for all coercions to $T$, the type coerced
from excludes $U$:
\[
T \rejects U \iff \forall A: A \coercedefto T \implies A \excludes U.
\]
Note that $T \rejects U$ implies $U \not\coercesto T$.

We say that $T$ is \emph{no less specific} than $U$, and write $T
\morespecificeq U$, if $T$ is a subtype of $U$ or $T$ excludes, can be
coerced to, and rejects $U$:
\[
T \morespecificeq U \iff
T \Ovrsubtype U \logicor
(T \excludes U \logicand T \coercesto U \logicand T \rejects U).
\]

The $\morespecificeq$ relation is reflexive and antisymmetric but not
necessarily transitive.  It is possible, for example, for
three types, $T$, $U$ and $V$, each excluding the other two,
to have coercions from $T$ to $U$ and from $U$ to $V$.  In
this case, $T \morespecificeq U$ and $U \morespecificeq V$ but
$T \not\morespecificeq V$.

Notice that if two tuple types have a bijective correspondence
between their element types then the $\morespecificeq$ relationship between
the tuple types is equivalent to applying the $\morespecificeq$
relation elementwise.

We say that $T$ is \emph{more specific} than $U$, and write $T
\morespecific U$, if $T \morespecificeq U \logicand T \neq U$.

We extend the definitions of no less specific and more specific to
declarations.  We say that a declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecificeq \Qs$.
Similarly, we say that a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
specific} than a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps)
\morespecificeq (\Qs_0, \Qs)$.  A declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more
specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$.
Similarly, a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more specific} than
a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps) \morespecific (\Qs_0,
\Qs)$.

#!/bin/bash
# count-run.sh <work-dir> <list-file> [shadow-classes-dir] [shards]: runs every file of <list-file> under
# `walk`, one JVM per test, and writes its output to <work-dir>/log/<test>.txt with an rc= secs= trailer.
# The shape of explorations/reviews/mie-probes/keep/nestprobe/run-tests.sh without its NestProbe shadow:
# each shard has its own FORTRESS_CACHES, so default_repository/ is never read or written and no two JVMs
# share a cache.  A shadow classes directory, if given, is put ahead of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath.
set -u
cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../.."                               # $FORTRESS_HOME
source explorations/experiment/env.sh
W=${1:?usage: count-run.sh <work-dir> <list-file> [shadow-classes-dir] [shards]}
L=${2:?usage: count-run.sh <work-dir> <list-file> [shadow-classes-dir] [shards]}
SH=${3:-}
N=${4:-4}
mkdir -p "$W/log"
CP=$(./bin/fortress_classpath 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
[ -n "$SH" ] && CP="$SH:$CP"
# one core per JVM, as the precedent: four run at once
FAST="-XX:+UseSerialGC -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1"
echo "start $(date -u +%FT%TZ) load: $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg) shadow: ${SH:-none}"
for i in $(seq 0 $((N-1))); do
  (
    C="$W/caches-$i"; T="$W/tmp-$i"; mkdir -p "$C" "$T"
    [ -f "$C/global.map" ] || printf '\0\0\0\0' > "$C/global.map"
    awk -v n=$N -v i=$i 'NR % n == i' "$L" | while read -r f; do
      t=$(basename "$f" .fss)
      grep -q '^rc=' "$W/log/$t.txt" 2>/dev/null && continue

#!/bin/bash
# count-run.sh <work-dir> <list-file> [shadow-classes-dir] [shards]: runs every file of <list-file> under
# `walk`, one JVM per test, and writes its output to <work-dir>/log/<test>.txt with an rc= secs= trailer.
# The shape of explorations/reviews/mie-probes/keep/nestprobe/run-tests.sh without its NestProbe shadow:
# each shard has its own FORTRESS_CACHES, so default_repository/ is never read or written and no two JVMs
# share a cache.  A shadow classes directory, if given, is put ahead of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath.
set -u
cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../.."                               # $FORTRESS_HOME
# env.sh without its rm of /tmp/fortress*rats, which a parallel agent's runs may be using
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH="/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH" FORTRESS_HOME="$(pwd)" FORTRESS_THREADS=1
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
W=${1:?usage: count-run.sh <work-dir> <list-file> [shadow-classes-dir] [shards]}
L=${2:?usage: count-run.sh <work-dir> <list-file> [shadow-classes-dir] [shards]}
SH=${3:-}
N=${4:-4}
mkdir -p "$W/log"
CP=$(./bin/fortress_classpath 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
[ -n "$SH" ] && CP="$SH:$CP"
# one core per JVM, as the precedent: four run at once
FAST="-XX:+UseSerialGC -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1"
echo "start $(date -u +%FT%TZ) load: $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg) shadow: ${SH:-none}"
for i in $(seq 0 $((N-1))); do
  (
    C="$W/caches-$i"; T="$W/tmp-$i"; mkdir -p "$C" "$T"
    [ -f "$C/global.map" ] || printf '\0\0\0\0' > "$C/global.map"
    awk -v n=$N -v i=$i 'NR % n == i' "$L" | while read -r f; do
      t=$(basename "$f" .fss)
      grep -q '^rc=' "$W/log/$t.txt" 2>/dev/null && continue
      start=$(date +%s)
      FORTRESS_CACHES="$C" timeout -k 10 600 \
        java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir="$T" $FAST -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell walk "$f" \
        < /dev/null > "$W/log/$t.txt" 2>&1
      rc=$?
      printf '\nrc=%s secs=%s\n' "$rc" "$(( $(date +%s) - start ))" >> "$W/log/$t.txt"
    done
  ) &
done
wait
rm -f ProjectFortress/tests/poem.out
echo "done $(date -u +%FT%TZ): $(grep -l '^rc=' "$W"/log/*.txt | wc -l) logs"
#!/bin/bash
# mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]: the two microGPT checks under walk, each from an empty
# private cache (FORTRESS_CACHES), each run from its own directory as its header says, both at once,
# with bin/fortress's own JVM (JAVA_FLAGS -Xmx4g -Xss64m) and FORTRESS_THREADS=<threads> (default 1).
# Output to <work-dir>/<name>.txt, headed by the machine line (machine.sh) and ended by rc=.
set -u
cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../.."                               # $FORTRESS_HOME
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH="/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH" FORTRESS_HOME="$(pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=${3:-1}
W=$(mkdir -p "${1:?usage}" && cd "$1" && pwd)
L=${2:?usage}
for f in explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlatCheck.fss explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptAplCheck.fss; do
  (
    t=$(basename "$f" .fss)
    C="$W/caches-$t"; T="$W/tmp-$t"; rm -rf "$C" "$T"; mkdir -p "$C" "$T"
    printf '\0\0\0\0' > "$C/global.map"
    {
      bash explorations/compile-ladder/rung-flat-tower/machine.sh "$L $t"
      start=$(date +%s)
      ( cd "$(dirname "$f")" && FORTRESS_CACHES="$C" JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$T" \
          timeout -k 10 5400 "$FORTRESS_HOME/bin/fortress" "$(basename "$f")" < /dev/null )
      echo "rc=$? secs=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))"
    } > "$W/$t.txt" 2>&1
  ) &
done
wait

#!/bin/bash
# Compile one probe with the bytecode compiler in the COMPILER's world (CompilerLibrary,
# where ZZ32, ZZ64 and RR64 are already siblings) into a private cache and run it,
# capturing to <Name>.comp.txt. The private cache is seeded from a library cache built
# once in library order at $SCRATCH/fqw-libcache (the flattening worker's libcache.sh,
# reused as it is: AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerAlgebra, CompilerLibrary, CompilerSystem).
#   explorations/reviews/sum-replacement-judgement/comp.sh <Name>
D="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
source "$D/../../experiment/env.sh"
N=$1
S=${SCRATCH:?set SCRATCH to a private directory}
L="$S/fqw-libcache"
C="$S/cache-comp-$N"
test -f "$L/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar" || SCRATCH="$S" "$D/../flattening-questions-ways/libcache.sh" || exit 1
rm -rf "$C"; cp -r "$L" "$C"
CP=$("$FORTRESS_HOME/bin/fortress_classpath" | tail -1)
cd "$D"
{
  echo "# comp.sh $N started $(date -u +%FT%TZ); tree $(git -C "$FORTRESS_HOME" rev-parse --short HEAD); nproc=$(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | sed 's/.*: //'); load $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | grep -m1 version); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS"
  echo "## fortress compile $N.fss (private cache, compiler's world)"
  JAVA_FLAGS="$JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches=$C" timeout -k 10 900 "$FORTRESS_HOME/bin/fortress" compile "$N.fss" 2>&1
  echo "compile rc=$?"
  echo "## run"
  timeout -k 10 600 java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches="$C" -cp "$C/bytecode_cache:$C/bytecode_cache/*:$C/nativewrapper_cache:$CP" com.sun.fortress.runtimeSystem.MainWrapper "$N" 2>&1 | grep -v "^Picked up JAVA_TOOL"
  echo "run rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
} > "$N.comp.txt" 2>&1
cat "$N.comp.txt"

#!/bin/bash
# Build the compiled path's library cache once, in library order, at $SCRATCH/fqw-libcache.
D="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
source "$D/../../experiment/env.sh"
L=${SCRATCH:-/tmp}/fqw-libcache
rm -rf "$L"; mkdir -p "$L"
cd "$FORTRESS_HOME"
for f in ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss \
         Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss Library/CompilerLibrary.fss Library/CompilerSystem.fss ; do
    JAVA_FLAGS="$JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches=$L" timeout -k 10 900 bin/fortress compile "$f" || exit 1
done
# Source this in every shell that runs Fortress:  source explorations/experiment/env.sh
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=1
# bin/fortress defaults to -Xmx256m (gap ledger row 67); the checks at 4 threads override FORTRESS_THREADS on the command line
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m"
# every grammar-importing run leaves a 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory behind (RatsUtil.getTempDir); 723 of them filled the disk allowance on 2026-09-15
rm -rf /tmp/fortress*rats 2>/dev/null

Here we present the trait \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and its methods.
Because \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} holds \EXP{0/0}, which is unordered with respect to every
rational value, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is neither totally ordered nor a field.
The original design of the rational types, in which \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
seventeen refined rational types are instantiations of one trait, is kept as a
superseded design in \secref{advanced-rationals}.
\revision{revival-numbers}{The Working Draft of February 2011 divided the
rationals into eighteen types: \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, the type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} that
adds the two infinities, the type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} that adds \EXP{0/0}, and
five refinements of each by sign, each a subtype of others and of the
corresponding real types, and it said that the type system tracks them through
arithmetic.
\Library\ never declared them, and the trait by which
\secref{advanced-rationals} defines them is refused by instantiation exclusion
(\secref{revival-rule}).
The text above describes the number types the library declares, siblings under
\TYP{Number}, with the coercions it declares; a subset such as the positive
values is tested at run time.
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} holds the values that \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}}
added, as the library's rational type does and as \chapref{operators} already
says (``For rational results, division by zero produces \EXP{1/0}'').
Because it holds \EXP{0/0}, the listing below no longer gives it the field and
order traits of the original design, which that design itself withheld from

trait DistributesOver[\E\] end

(** The identity of + and of juxtaposition for the number type named by the
    static argument alone, with no element in hand: the typecase over a
    %() -> T% witness that %array1% uses.  Each type is tested before its
    supertypes. **)
additiveIdentity[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\](): T =
    typecase __thrower[\T\] of
        () -> ZZ32 => cast[\T\](0)
        () -> ZZ64 => cast[\T\](widen(0))
        () -> NN32 => cast[\T\](unsigned(0))
        () -> NN64 => cast[\T\](widen(unsigned(0)))
        () -> ZZ => cast[\T\](big(0))
        () -> QQ => cast[\T\](Ratio(0, 1))
        () -> RR32 => cast[\T\](narrow(0.0))
        () -> RR64 => cast[\T\](0.0)
        else => 0
    end

multiplicativeIdentity[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\](): T =
    typecase __thrower[\T\] of
        () -> ZZ32 => cast[\T\](1)
        () -> ZZ64 => cast[\T\](widen(1))
        () -> NN32 => cast[\T\](unsigned(1))
        () -> NN64 => cast[\T\](widen(unsigned(1)))
        () -> ZZ => cast[\T\](big(1))
        () -> QQ => cast[\T\](Ratio(1, 1))
        () -> RR32 => cast[\T\](narrow(1.0))
        () -> RR64 => cast[\T\](1.0)
        else => 1
    end

object SumProdReductionPair[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\] extends ReductionPair[\T,T\]
    getter outer() = SumReduction[\T\]
    getter inner() = ProdReduction[\T\]
(* WitnessComp -- the compiled path in the compiler's world (CompilerLibrary, where
   ZZ32, ZZ64 and RR64 are siblings): the library's device for choosing by a static
   argument alone, a typecase over a () -> T witness, with each branch's value put
   through cast[\T\] so that the checker sees T (Q1ZeroWitnessComp failed without it:
   "body has type OR(FloatLiteral,ZZ64,IntLiteral,BottomType), but declared return
   type is T"). Does the checker accept it, and does the compiled run choose the branch
   by T's run-time descriptor? *)
component WitnessComp
export Executable

witness[\T\](): T = throw InvalidRange

zeroOf[\T\](): T =
    typecase witness[\T\] of
        () -> ZZ32 => cast[\T\](0)
        () -> ZZ64 => cast[\T\](widen(0))
        () -> RR64 => cast[\T\](0.0)
        else => throw InvalidRange
    end

run(): () = do
    println("zeroOf[\\ZZ32\\]() = " zeroOf[\ZZ32\]())
    println("zeroOf[\\ZZ64\\]() = " zeroOf[\ZZ64\]())
    println("zeroOf[\\RR64\\]() = " zeroOf[\RR64\]())
    println("zeroOf[\\RR64\\]() + 1.5 = " (zeroOf[\RR64\]() + 1.5))
    println("zeroOf[\\ZZ32\\]() + 7 = " (zeroOf[\ZZ32\]() + 7))
  end
end

content.content: | 351 | **a `catch` or `typecase` clause binding cannot be read in the clause body on the compiled path**: `CodeGen.forTry` (`CodeGen.java:2016`) takes the catch name at `:2042` (`Id name = _catch.getName();`) and never uses it; the clause body is compiled at `:2057` (`clause.getBody().accept(this);`) with nothing added to the local environment, and the team's comment at `:2035` says why — "We really should have desugared this into typecase, but for now…". A reference to the name reaches `forVarRef` (`:5953-5974` in the rung's tree), where `getLocalVarOrNull` returns null and the class name is built with `NamingCzar.jvmClassForToplevelDecl`, so the run asks for the singleton class of a top-level variable that nobody emits. `forTypecase` (`:2112-2146`) is the second site: it never reads `c.getName()`, although `TypecaseClause` carries it (`ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast:1659`, example at `:1656-1657`). Two sites, one cause | NEGATIVE-VERIFIED | implementation gap | `Specification/basic/expressions/try.tex:56-60`, "the exception value is bound to the identifier specified in the `catch` clause", with the grammar at `:22`, settles the catch site against the compiled run; for the typecase site the 1.0 prose covers only the `typecase x of` spelling (`basic/expressions/typecase.tex:55-62`, `:88-98`, note at `:15`), so the per-clause `Id :` form is silent-specification territory and the interpreter plus the AST's own example are the evidence | `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-tryatomic/probes/catch-binding.txt` (compile exit 0, run exit 1, `NoClassDefFoundError: CatchBindingRef$e`; under `walk` exit 0 and `caught: Try/atomic failure`) and `probes/typecase-binding.txt` (the same on `$x`; under `walk` `typecase: 7`); gated as an expected failure at the catch site by `ProjectFortress/library_tests/XXXClauseBindingRungB.fss` with `XXXClauseBindingRungB.test` and `ClauseBindingRungBLink.test` | ours (rung B, 2026-09-20) | The fix: give the clause binding a local for the duration of the clause body, the shape `CodeGen` already uses at `:2849` and `:3941` (`new VarCodeGen.LocalVar(…)` then `addLocalVar`), at both sites. Not repaired in rung B because `CodeGen.java` was rung X's file in this batch (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-2.md:77`); every `CodeGen.java` number above is re-anchored to the landed tree except `:5953-5974`, which is marked above as the rung's own tree and is `:5969-5990` in the landed file. Corrected by the merged-diff review of 2026-09-20: rung X inserted at two places in that file, so the offset is not uniform — one line, the `import` at `:52-53`, for every citation above `CodeGen.java:5951`, and sixteen below it, `importedVarIsMutable` being fifteen more lines at `:5954-5968`. Every citation in rung B's own report, record and probes above `:5951` therefore reads one lower than the landed file, and its `forVarRef` numbers read sixteen lower. Nothing in either corpus referenced a clause binding before this rung, which is why 5,397 commits and three campaigns had not seen it. |
